questions.prompt: Which scheduling algorithm gives the CPU to the process that arrived first?
questions.explain: First come, first served: a simple FIFO queue.

questions.prompt: What is the convoy effect?
options: Short processes waiting behind a long one in FCFS
questions.explain: A long CPU burst at the head of the queue delays everyone behind it, so the average waiting time grows.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time?
questions.explain: Shortest job first is optimal for the average waiting time (if the burst lengths are known).

questions.prompt: What is a cooperative (non-preemptive) scheduler?
options: One that never changes the priorities
One that only chooses another process when the running one waits or ends
One that shares the CPU in equal slices
questions.explain: A preemptive scheduler can also take the CPU away from a running process (a time slice ends, a better process arrives).

questions.prompt: The time a process spends in the ready queue is its {{0}} time.
questions.explain: Turnaround time is from arrival to finish; waiting time is only the time spent ready but not running.

questions.prompt: For a process with one CPU burst and no I/O, turnaround time equals:
questions.explain: Turnaround = finish - arrival = time waiting + time running.

questions.prompt: A round-robin scheduler with a VERY large quantum behaves like:
questions.explain: Nobody is ever preempted, so processes run to the end in arrival order.

questions.prompt: Priority scheduling can leave a low-priority process without CPU forever. What is that problem and its cure?
options: The convoy effect, solved with round robin
questions.explain: Aging raises the priority of processes that have waited a long time.

questions.prompt: FCFS with bursts P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 ms, all arriving at time 0 in that order. What is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: P1 waits 0, P2 waits 24, P3 waits 27: (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17 ms. In the order 3, 3, 24 it would be 3 ms: the convoy effect.

questions.prompt: The same three processes arrive in the order P2 = 3, P3 = 3, P1 = 24 (all at time 0). What is the average waiting time with FCFS?
questions.explain: They wait 0, 3 and 6 ms: (0 + 3 + 6) / 3 = 3 ms.

questions.prompt: Cooperative SJF with P1 (arrives 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4). Which process runs right after P1 finishes at time 7?
questions.explain: At time 7 the ready processes are P2 (4), P3 (1) and P4 (4): the shortest is P3.

questions.prompt: Cooperative SJF on that same set: what is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: The waits are 0, 6, 3 and 7: 16 / 4 = 4 ms.

questions.prompt: Preemptive SJF (shortest remaining time) on the same set: which process is running at time 4?
questions.explain: At time 4, P3 arrives with a burst of 1, less than what P1 (5) and P2 (2) have left, so it takes the CPU.

questions.prompt: Preemptive SJF on that set: what is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: The waits are 9, 1, 0 and 2: 12 / 4 = 3 ms, better than the cooperative 4 ms.

questions.prompt: Round robin, quantum 20 ms. P1 = 53, P2 = 17, P3 = 68, P4 = 24 (all arrive at 0). What is the waiting time of P2?
questions.explain: P1 runs 0-20, then P2 runs 20-37 and finishes: it waited 20 ms (its turnaround is 37 and its burst is 17).

questions.prompt: Same system: what is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: The waits are 81, 20, 94 and 97: 292 / 4 = 73 ms.

questions.prompt: Round robin, quantum 4 ms, processes P1 = 10, P2 = 3, P3 = 5 (all arrive at 0). Put the CPU slices in order.
questions.explain: P2 finishes in its first slice (3 < 4). P3 needs two slices and P1 three. The finish times are 18, 7 and 16.

questions.prompt: In that round-robin schedule, what is the waiting time of P3 (burst 5)?
questions.explain: P3 finishes at 16 and runs for 5 ms, so it waited 16 - 5 = 11 ms.

questions.prompt: Match each algorithm with its main idea.
pairs: equal time slices in a circular queue
processes move between queues with different algorithms
questions.explain: These are the algorithms of the topic.

questions.prompt: In SJF the next burst is estimated as tau(n+1) = alpha * t(n) + (1 - alpha) * tau(n). With alpha = 1 the estimate is just the {{0}} real burst.
questions.explain: alpha = 1 forgets the history; alpha = 0 ignores the new measurements and keeps the old estimate.

questions.prompt: With alpha = 0.5, a previous estimate tau = 10 and a real burst t = 6, what is the next estimate?
Which scheduler decides which new processes enter the ready queue?
questions.explain: The long-term scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming; it runs rarely, so it can be slow.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of a context switch?
options: Time in which the CPU does no useful work
questions.explain: Too many switches (a tiny quantum) waste CPU time.

questions.prompt: Is each scheduling policy preemptive or cooperative?
questions.explain: Preemptive policies can take the CPU from a running process; cooperative ones wait until it ends or blocks.

questions.prompt: A system has three queues: queue 0 is round robin with quantum 20, queue 1 round robin with quantum 40 and queue 2 FCFS. A new process enters queue 0. It uses its whole quantum without finishing. Where does it go?
questions.explain: In multilevel feedback queues a process that exhausts its quantum is demoted to the next queue.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of multilevel feedback queues?
options: To keep short and interactive processes in the higher-priority queues while long CPU-bound ones sink
questions.explain: A process that uses little CPU stays up; one that always uses its whole quantum drops.

questions.prompt: A process is in the middle of a disk burst. What does it need from the CPU while it lasts?
questions.explain: Nothing. A disk burst is done by the disk, not by the CPU, so the CPU can run another ready process meanwhile. Overlapping the two is the whole point of multiprogramming.
options: Nothing: the CPU can run other processes meanwhile
The CPU, because it has to wait actively for the disk
One CPU quantum at a time
Only the CPU if its priority is high

questions.prompt: Put the life of a process that has one CPU burst, one disk burst and one more CPU burst in order.
questions.explain: It is ready after arriving, runs, asks for the disk and may have to queue for it, uses it, becomes ready again for its last CPU burst and finally terminates.
items: Its CPU burst ends and it asks for the disk (W if the disk is busy)
It is ready again (L) and runs its last CPU burst (E)

questions.prompt: Which process does a FCFS disk serve next?
questions.explain: The one whose request arrived first. The disk of these problems does not look at priorities or burst lengths; it only keeps the order of the requests.
options: The one with the shortest disk burst
The one that has used the CPU least
The one that asked for the disk first
The one with the best CPU priority

questions.prompt: With round robin and a quantum of 20 ms, a process runs a CPU burst of 8 ms and then asks for the disk. What happens to the rest of its quantum?
questions.explain: The process gives up the CPU when its burst ends, so the CPU is assigned to the next ready process at once with a fresh quantum. Quanta are not saved for later.
options: The remaining 12 ms are added to the quantum of the next burst
The process goes to the end of the ready queue
The CPU stays idle until the 20 ms are over
Nothing is waited for: the CPU goes to the next ready process right away

questions.prompt: With preemptive priorities, a process comes back from the disk with a better priority than the one that is running. What happens at that instant?
questions.explain: A process that becomes ready with a strictly better priority preempts the running one, wherever it comes from (new arrival or return from the disk). The preempted process goes back to the ready queue with what was left of its burst.
options: It goes to the end of the disk queue
It waits until the running burst ends
It waits until the end of the quantum

questions.prompt: In a system with a high-priority FCFS queue and a low-priority round robin queue, a high process preempts a low one. Where does the low process go, and what does it keep?
questions.explain: Being preempted is not its fault, so the scheduler puts it back at the head of its queue and remembers how much of the quantum it had left, so that it is not punished.
options: To the head of the low queue, remembering the rest of its quantum
To the end of the low queue, with a fresh quantum

questions.prompt: In a multilevel feedback queue, why is a process that uses its whole quantum moved to a lower queue?
questions.explain: A process that uses all its quantum is probably CPU-bound. Moving it down keeps the short, interactive or I/O-bound processes (which give the CPU back early) in the higher queues, where they are served first.
options: Because the quantum of the lower queue is shorter
It looks CPU-bound, and the short or I/O-bound processes should be served first
Because it has been waiting for the disk

questions.prompt: One process is CPU-bound and long, another uses 2 ms of CPU and then the disk, over and over. With FCFS on the CPU, what is the typical problem?
questions.explain: The short one has to wait behind the long CPU burst each time it comes back, so the disk is idle most of the time and the overall use of the machine is poor: the convoy effect.
options: The short process never asks for the disk
The disk stays idle while the short process waits behind the long CPU burst (convoy effect)
Nothing: FCFS is optimal for this mix

questions.prompt: FCFS on the CPU and on the disk. P1 arrives at 0 and has bursts CPU 10, disk 10, CPU 10. P2 arrives at 5 and has a single CPU burst of 10. P1 terminates at t = {{0}}.
questions.explain: P1 runs 0-10 and uses the disk 10-20. P2 arrived at 5 and runs 10-20. At 20 P1 is ready again and runs 20-30.

questions.prompt: Same system: P1 arrives at 0 with CPU 10, disk 10, CPU 10; P2 arrives at 5 with a single CPU burst of 10. In ms, P2 spends {{0}} ms in the ready state (waiting for the CPU) before it first runs.
questions.explain: P2 arrives at 5, but the CPU is busy with P1 until 10, so it waits 5 ms.

questions.prompt: Why does it make the CPU busier to have several processes in memory that use the disk?
questions.explain: While one process waits for the disk, the CPU can run another: with enough processes it almost never has to wait with nothing to do.
options: Because the processes share their quantum
While one waits for the disk another can use the CPU
Because the disk makes the CPU faster
Because the disk runs the processes itself

questions.prompt: Match each scheduling algorithm with the property or problem it is known for.
questions.explain: FCFS suffers the convoy effect; SJF gives the minimum average waiting time (but needs the burst length and can starve long jobs); round robin shares the CPU in turns of one quantum; priorities can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes.
pairs: convoy effect: short processes wait behind a long one
minimum average waiting time, but long jobs can starve
everyone gets the CPU in turns of one quantum
low-priority processes may starve; aging helps

questions.prompt: Which statements about the quantum of round robin are true?
questions.explain: A huge quantum makes round robin behave like FCFS. A tiny one makes the processes share the CPU almost evenly, but the context switches then take a large part of the time.
options: With a very small quantum the context switches cost a lot
The quantum is the time a process may wait in the queue
With a very large quantum it behaves like FCFS
A process always uses its whole quantum
A process whose burst ends before the quantum is over leaves the CPU at that moment
option_notes: False: the quantum limits the time ON the CPU.
False: it leaves earlier if its burst ends or it waits for the disk.

questions.prompt: Sort these processes by their finish time under non-preemptive SJF on one CPU. All arrive at time 0: P1 needs 8 ms, P2 needs 3 ms, P3 needs 5 ms, P4 needs 1 ms.
questions.explain: SJF runs them from the shortest to the longest: P4 (1), P2 (3), P3 (5) and P1 (8).
